meta.title: Solution Sets to Inequalities with Two Variables
meta.description: Graph linear inequalities in two variables as shaded half-planes with solid or dashed boundary lines.
meta.pageDescription: Graph linear inequalities in two variables, use test points, and shade feasible half-planes.
meta.author: Hesten's Learning Team

overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 21
overview.text: In this lesson, you will graph linear inequalities in two variables (such as $y < 2x - 1$ or $Ax + By \ge C$). A linear boundary divides the Cartesian plane into two half-planes. You will master using a test point (such as $(0, 0)$) to decide which half-plane contains the solutions.
outcomes: Graph the solution set to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane.
Differentiate between solid boundary lines (inclusive $\le, \ge$) and dashed boundary lines (strict $<, >$).
Select and evaluate a test point (e.g., $(0, 0)$) to identify which side of the boundary to shade.
overview.teacherInsight: Highlight that if the boundary line passes through the origin $(0, 0)$, students must select an alternate test point like $(0, 1)$ or $(1, 0)$ to test which half-plane to shade.

content.html:
Rules for Graphing Two-Variable Inequalities

Boundary Line Style

$$\text{Strict } (<, >): \text{Dashed} \quad | \quad \text{Inclusive } (\le, \ge): \text{Solid}$$

Solid lines include points on the boundary; dashed lines indicate the boundary itself is excluded from solutions.

Test-Point Verification

$$\text{Test } (0, 0) \to \text{If True: Shade Origin Side}$$

If $(0,0)$ evaluates to True, shade the side containing $(0,0)$. If False, shade the opposite side.

vocabulary.definition: The region of a coordinate plane on one side of an infinite boundary line.
The line dividing the coordinate plane into two half-planes in an inequality graph.
A coordinate pair (not on the boundary line) substituted into an inequality to determine which half-plane contains solutions.

practiceQuestions.question: Which inequality and graphical representation accurately models the statement: 'The sum of two numbers is less than 10'?
options: $x + y < 10$; graphed with a dashed boundary line $y = -x + 10$ and shading below the line
$x + y \le 10$; graphed with a solid boundary line $y = -x + 10$ and shading above the line
$xy < 10$; graphed as a hyperbola with shading in the first quadrant
$x - y < 10$; graphed with a vertical dashed line at $x = 10$
practiceQuestions.explanation: From the official Eureka Math Exit Ticket Key: 'The sum of two numbers is less than 10' translates to $x + y < 10 \implies y < -x + 10$. The strict inequality requires a dashed line (points on the line are not included), and 'less than' shades the half-plane below.

practiceQuestions.question: Is the coordinate point $(5, 5)$ included in the solution set of $x + y < 10$, and why?
options: No, because $5 + 5 = 10$, which is not strictly less than 10.
Yes, because both numbers are positive.
No, because coordinates must be negative.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Substitute $(5, 5)$: $5 + 5 = 10 < 10$ is a false statement. Points lying directly on the dashed boundary line are excluded from strict inequalities.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 21 Exit Ticket: Two-Variable Linear Inequalities and Their Half-Planes
exitTicket.prompt: What pairs of numbers satisfy the statement: The sum of two numbers is less than 10? Create an inequality with two variables to represent this situation, and describe the graph of its solution set.
exitTicket.solution:
Let x = one number, and let y = second number.
Inequality: x + y < 10 (or y < -x + 10).
Graph: A dashed boundary line along y = -x + 10 (dashed because the inequality is strictly less than, not <=), with the entire half-plane shaded below the line.

guidedExercises.title: Example 1: Graphing Two-Variable Inequalities and Half-Planes
guidedExercises.problem: Graph the solution set of $2x + y < 4$ on the Cartesian coordinate plane.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Step 1: Graph the boundary line $2x + y = 4$ as dashed (because strict inequality $<$ excludes the line). Step 2: Test a test point (such as $(0, 0)$) to decide which half-plane to shade.

steps.label: Test the origin $(0, 0)$
steps.explanation: Since $(0, 0)$ makes the statement true, shade the half-plane containing the origin.

guidedExercises.finalAnswer: \text{Dashed line } y = -2x + 4 \text{ with the region below/left (containing origin) shaded.}
guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Drawing a solid boundary line instead of a dashed line for strict inequalities ($<$ or $>$). Solid lines are only used for $\le$ or $\ge$.
